answer:
Use FEniCS legacy (dolfin) to solve small-strain linear elasticity in 2D with the plane-stress assumption and unit thickness.
Define the domain as the unit square [0,1]x[0,1] with the bottom-left quadrant [0,0.5]x[0,5] removed, giving an L-shape with a re-entrant corner at (0.5, 0.5); note in the implementation that this corner placement is an interpretation consistent with the traction profile, since the requirement only states "1x1 outer - 0.5x0.5 inner".
Mesh the domain with 64 elements per edge.
Use material properties E = 70e9 Pa, nu = 0.33, rho = 2700 kg/m^3, and g = 9.81 m/s^2.
Formulate the plane-stress constitutive law using the reduced plane-stress stiffness matrix built from E and nu.
Use a vector-valued displacement function space (P1 or P2 Lagrange elements are acceptable; state the choice in the implementation).
Apply gravity as a body force rho*g in the negative y-direction included in the variational form.
Clamp the left boundary x = 0 (which spans y in [0.5, 1]) with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions on both displacement components.
Apply a normal traction on the outer right edge x = 1 with sigma_yy(y) = -2.65e4*y Pa, evaluated using the global y-coordinate so the traction varies linearly from 0 Pa at y = 0 to -2.65e4 Pa (compressive, downward) at y = 1; do not evaluate the profile with x, since on x = 1 that would wrongly give a constant traction.
Leave the re-entrant inner boundaries (the notch surfaces) and all other outer boundaries traction-free.
Assemble the linear system and solve it with a direct linear solver.
Compute the in-plane Cauchy stress components sigma_xx, sigma_yy, and sigma_xy from the plane-stress constitutive law and the solved displacement field.
Compute the von Mises stress from the in-plane stress components only.
Output the displacement distribution (both components) and the stress distributions including von Mises over the L-shaped domain, suitable for visualization or post-processing.
